cases.suppression: The harm in the case was done by the Sudanese army and the government-linked Popular Defence Forces (Janjaweed).
cases.killed_note: Al Jazeera, citing the UN, gives about 300,000 dead in the Sudanese war in 2002-2008. These deaths were caused by the Sudanese state and militia, and the verdict concerned three survivors, so none are counted here.

lvwhy.finance: Letters of credit and dollar access let Sudan sell exports and receive the money.

cases.title: BNP Paribas's Banking for Sudan and the Darfur Verdict
cases.place: Darfur and other parts of Sudan
cases.point: El Fasher, Darfur, as a marker for the violence in the case (approximate; the three plaintiffs were not tied to this town in the pages read)

lenders.name: BNP Paribas
lenders.role: French bank. Did business in Sudan from the late 1990s until 2009 and gave letters of credit that let Sudan meet its import and export commitments (Al Jazeera). The US Justice Department says it moved about $6.4 billion through the US for sanctioned Sudanese entities from July 2006 to June 2007. These were banking services, not a loan.

cases.conditions: Letters of credit and US-dollar processing through the bank's Geneva office, not a project loan. BNP pleaded guilty on 9 July 2014 in a Manhattan federal court to conspiring to break US sanctions covering Sudan, Iran and Cuba, and agreed to total penalties of $8.9736 billion: a plea, not only a settlement (US Justice Department). That case treated the sanctions breach as the crime and did not concern harm to Sudanese civilians.
cases.community: Three Sudanese refugees, now US citizens, testified that Sudanese soldiers and the Janjaweed militia tortured them, burned them with cigarettes and slashed them with a knife; the woman also said she was sexually assaulted. Al Jazeera, citing the UN, reports that the war killed about 300,000 people between 2002 and 2008 and displaced 2.5 million.
cases.outcome: A Manhattan federal jury, after a trial of more than five weeks before Judge Alvin Hellerstein, found BNP liable and awarded $20.75 million: Abulgasim Abdalla $6.7 million, Entesar Osman Kashef $7.3 million, Turjuman Adam $6.75 million (Hausfeld, 17 October 2025). It found that the bank's conscious help to the Bashir government facilitated abuses that injured the three. On 7 January 2026 the judge denied BNP's post-trial motions and certified the verdict for appeal (Domain-b). The appeal is pending at the US Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit: BNP filed its opening brief on 22 May 2026, the Swiss government filed in support of BNP, and human rights groups filed in support of the plaintiffs by August 2026 (BNP Paribas, ECCHR). The class covers more than 20,000 Sudanese refugees in the US; the verdict so far covers three people.

cases.ecosystem: Salonga is a forest park of over 36,000 sq km and a UNESCO World Heritage Site (Rainforest Foundation UK).
cases.suppression: A senior park official told investigator Willy Elua he might not leave the park alive, and police then warned him rangers planned to kill him. Investigators got eight days where one said three weeks were needed, and WWF and government partners did not want them to interview a villager shot in the leg (BuzzFeed News).
cases.killed_note: Gaby Simba, tortured to death by guards in 2015, when WWF already co-managed the park (BuzzFeed News). The WWF-commissioned investigation confirmed 3 murders by rangers in 2002-2016 (Rainforest Foundation UK); the other two are not dated in the pages read, so they cannot be placed inside the donors' funding and are not counted. Rainforest Foundation UK's wider count of at least 9 killed is also not counted. A fisherman found dead in late 2019 was referred to a military tribunal (Mongabay); not counted.

lvwhy.land: Rangers enforced a ban on fishing and hunting in the park.
lvwhy.project: Grants paid for ranger support and park management.

cases.title: Salonga National Park: Abuse by Donor-Backed Rangers
cases.point: Monkoto, on the edge of the park (approximate; the sources do not name the villages)

lenders.name: USAID (grant)
lenders.role: The park is funded by the US and German governments. USAID has spent 'millions' in Salonga in recent years, including on rangers and law enforcement; no figure or years given (BuzzFeed News).

lenders.name: KfW, German state development bank (grant)
lenders.role: Gave more than 5 million euros to Salonga since 2016 and pledged another 1.3 million the year before the 2019 report (BuzzFeed News). This money starts after the 2015 killing. Suspended all funding to WWF in 2019.

lenders.name: WWF
lenders.role: Worked in Salonga since 2005 and became co-manager with the Congolese parks agency ICCN in 2015; trained rangers and paid salary bonuses for meeting patrol targets (Mongabay on the independent panel).

cases.conditions: Donor grants paid for park management and ranger support through WWF and ICCN. About 700 communities surround the park, with an estimated 130,000 people in the corridor between its two halves (Rainforest Foundation UK).
cases.community: A draft report commissioned by WWF and the Congolese government found rangers stopped four women carrying fish by a river, whipped them and raped them; two were pregnant and a nurse said one later miscarried. The report gives 12 rangers as implicated. In 2015 Gaby Simba was arrested and tortured to death when guards could not catch his brother, which investigators said 'can be considered as premeditated murder'. Rangers tied villagers' penises with fishing line (BuzzFeed News). Rainforest Foundation UK says the investigation confirmed 3 murders, 6 rapes and 3 men tortured in 2002-2016, and that its own and local investigators count at least 9 killed, 9 women raped and 63 tortured or abused. A 2018 survey of 231 people in 11 villages found nearly one in four said rangers had physically attacked them (Mongabay).
cases.outcome: WWF said implicated rangers were suspended and joint patrols with the military ended. KfW suspended funding and Germany put WWF money on hold in 2019. More than $12 million in financing for conservation groups in the Congo Basin was suspended, and the US Interior Department said it would stop funding conservation there. A panel WWF appointed, chaired by Navi Pillay, reported on 24 November 2020 that WWF country managers failed to follow up credible allegations; it found no evidence WWF directed the abuses (Mongabay, BuzzFeed News).

USAID said it raised the reports with WWF and urged a full response. Amounts of US money for Salonga are not public in the pages read, and the rangers' employer is not stated in the BuzzFeed report.

cases.killed_note: The Oakland Institute reported 11 people killed in circumstances involving the Trust. A review commissioned by The Nature Conservancy, a Trust funder, found no evidence against the rangers, and an enquiry led by Dr Paul Kanyinke Sena said none of the allegations could be concretely substantiated. cases.title: Northern Rangelands Trust Conservancies in Isiolo
cases.place: Biliqo Bulesa and Cherab conservancies, Isiolo County, Kenya
cases.point: Merti, Isiolo County, near the two conservancies (approximate)

lenders.name: USAID (grant)
lenders.role: Gave the Northern Rangelands Trust nearly $20 million from 2015 to 2020; support continued through 2024 and ended in January 2025, after which the Trust laid off nearly 100 staff (Mongabay). The page does not say what the money paid for or whether it reached these two conservancies.

cases.conditions: Donor grants paid the Trust, which supports community conservancies; The Nature Conservancy is also a funder. The Trust's carbon project sold more than 1.5 million credits (REDD-Monitor), worth tens of millions of dollars (Mongabay); buyers are not named, and buying credits alone does not count as a link here. Biliqo Bulesa was set up in 2007.
cases.community: 165 community members sued in September 2021. On 24 January 2025 the Environment and Land Court at Isiolo found the two conservancies were set up on unregistered community land without proper consultation or consent. The plaintiffs accused the Trust of arming rangers and alleged violence, loss of life and forced disappearances; the pages read do not say the court found these proven. The Oakland Institute (2021) reported 11 people killed in circumstances involving the Trust.
cases.outcome: The court permanently barred the Trust and partners from conservancy operations, including deploying rangers, in the two conservancies and told the county to help register the land. A stay was refused in April 2025 and the case is now in Kenya's appeals process. Verra suspended the carbon project in March 2023 and again in May 2025, saying the ruling led to the second suspension.

The inquiry lists two poisonings, a suspected snake bite, malaria, a drowning, a probable brain haemorrhage and a viral fever, and found the deaths 'most probably unrelated to the vaccine' though causes could not be fully established (Full Fact). lvwhy.project: A foundation grant paid for vaccinating girls under a design with weak consent and monitoring.

cases.title: Gates-Funded HPV Vaccine Projects in Khammam and Vadodara
cases.place: Khammam, Andhra Pradesh, and Vadodara, Gujarat, India
cases.point: Khammam town, in one of the two project districts

lenders.name: Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation (grant)
lenders.role: Funded the projects run by PATH (Indian Journal of Medical Ethics). The official inquiry committee did not document the funding or money spent (same source).

cases.conditions: PATH, a Seattle-based organisation, ran 'demonstration projects' with the Indian Council of Medical Research and the two state governments. Gardasil and Cervarix were donated by Merck and GlaxoSmithKline.
cases.community: About 23,000 girls aged 10 to 14 were vaccinated in mid-2009 (Indian Journal of Medical Ethics; PATH says 23,500, Full Fact about 24,000). The parliamentary committee found consent forms 'incomplete and inaccurate' and that Andhra Pradesh told hostel wardens to sign for parents. It found the design caused gross under-reporting of adverse events, and approval papers had no section for serious adverse events (Down To Earth, Indian Journal of Medical Ethics). The projects stopped in 2010 after reports of deaths.
cases.outcome: The projects were suspended in 2010. The 72nd report of the Parliamentary Standing Committee, tabled on 30 August 2013, found the project was a clinical trial that broke the rules, cited 'serious dereliction of duty', recommended that the health ministry act against PATH, and said the human rights and child rights commissions could take up the matter.

cases.title: US-Funded Syphilis and Gonorrhea Experiments in Guatemala
cases.point: Guatemala City, home of the national penitentiary and mental hospital used in the study (approximate)

lenders.name: US National Institutes of Health (grant)
lenders.role: Gave a grant to the Pan American Sanitary Bureau, which funded several Guatemalan government ministries (US Department of Health and Human Services fact sheet).

lenders.name: Pan American Sanitary Bureau
lenders.role: Passed the US money to Guatemalan ministries and collaborated in the study (HHS, CDC).

cases.conditions: The study sought to test whether penicillin could prevent sexually transmitted diseases. Dr John Cutler of the US Public Health Service led it on site.
cases.community: A US presidential commission counted 1,308 people intentionally exposed to syphilis, gonorrhea or chancroid (Clinician.com), among them prisoners, soldiers, psychiatric patients and sex workers. They were not told and did not consent. Under 700 received documented treatment (Al Jazeera). CDC's review of the records: 427 of 696 exposed to syphilis were judged infected, 234 of 772 to gonorrhea, 138 of 142 to chancroid. Seven women with epilepsy were injected below the skull and developed meningitis (Al Jazeera). 1,384 orphan children had blood tests and some had lumbar punctures (Clinician.com).
cases.outcome: Susan Reverby of Wellesley College found the records. President Obama apologised to Guatemala's president in October 2010 and ordered a review; the commission went through about 125,000 pages of records and called the study an institutional failure.

cases.title: Donor Money at the Somsanga Drug Detention Centre
cases.point: Vientiane Municipality, under whose authority the centre sits (approximate)

lenders.name: US government (grants)
lenders.role: $145,786 for a clinic in 2001-2003; US Embassy paid for a women's facility opened February 2008 and two male buildings for about 150 in 2009-2010, with bid invitations that included fences; State Department INL funded a $242,837 UNODC project in 2008 to mid-2011 (Human Rights Watch).

lenders.name: UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC)
lenders.role: Built a clinic with the US money in 2001-2003, paid for a $95,200 renovation in 2009 and gave staff drug-counselling training in 2004-2006.

lenders.name: Japan, Singapore, Germany and Australia (grants)
lenders.role: Japan's embassy helped build a treatment block (Lao state press); Singapore helped raise $22,500 for a motorbike repair centre; Germany paid $10,000 for gym equipment in 2009; Australia gave $9,300 for a library in 2010 (Lao state press).

cases.conditions: Grants paid for buildings, fences, staff training and programmes inside the locked centre.
cases.community: Human Rights Watch found detention without trial or appeal. Detainees were locked in rooms more than 20 hours a day at weekends. Room captains beat detainees, sometimes on police orders. Punishments included being sent to work in a septic tank; one detainee was handcuffed to a volleyball net pole from about 1 pm until 5 or 6 pm. Management reported 1,087 detainees in mid-2011, and 4,151 people were held in 2008-2010. Former detainees estimated that between 1 in 5 and up to half were not drug users; others held were beggars, homeless people, street children and people with mental disabilities. Five of 12 former detainees interviewed saw suicides or attempts. All 12 had been held within two years of their interviews.
cases.outcome: HRW published its report on 11 October 2011 and asked donors to call for the centre's closure. The US State Department's narcotics bureau, the US, Japanese and Australian embassies did not reply; those that did said they knew of no abuse. The EU said it does not fund Somsanga.

sources.title: Somsanga's Secrets: arbitrary detention, physical abuse, and suicide inside a Lao drug detention center

cases.confidence_note: Rests on one field report by Human Rights Watch, based on 12 former detainees, with no second source for the abuse. UNODC said it had not received reports of staff physically abusing detainees, though it confirmed one death in custody. Some Japanese and Australian figures come from the Lao state press agency. The report gives no exact dates for the abuses, so they cannot be matched to particular grants; testimony and the 2008-2011 grants overlap.

cases.suppression: Many people were arrested without warrant, sometimes at a relative's request or in police round-ups, and had no lawyer (Human Rights Watch).

cases.title: UNICEF Funding and the Choam Chao Youth Centre
cases.point: Choam Chao area of Phnom Penh (approximate)

lenders.name: UNICEF (grant)
lenders.role: Gave 'limited funding' through the Ministry of Social Affairs and supported the centre from 2006 as part of juvenile justice reform; no amount given (UNICEF). Stopped funding after confirming abuse reports (Human Rights Watch, 2013).

cases.conditions: Part of a juvenile justice reform strategy, per UNICEF. A European Union representative called for an investigation into whether EU money to UNICEF supported rights violations (Human Rights Watch).
cases.community: Human Rights Watch's January 2010 report on Cambodian drug detention centres recorded beatings, electric shocks, forced labour, rape and forced blood donation. At Choam Chao a 16-year-old described witnessing whippings. UNICEF's own inquiry found credible evidence of ill-treatment by older children supervising younger boys, and of slapping and hitting by a temporary staff member.
cases.outcome: The government stopped using youth supervisors, dismissed the staff member and suspended new referrals (UNICEF, 8 June 2010). The centre stopped operating in mid-2010 and its buildings were demolished in late 2012. A 2012 joint statement of 12 UN agencies urged closure of such centres. HRW said in 2013 that three centres had closed since 2010, Choam Chao among them, while detainee numbers stayed about the same.

cases.title: Plan Colombia: US-Financed Aerial Spraying of Glyphosate
cases.place: Putumayo and Nariño, Colombia, and the Ecuador border
cases.point: Puerto Asís area, Putumayo, in a heavily sprayed border department (approximate)

lenders.name: US State Department, Plan Colombia
lenders.role: The US finances the spraying and partly uses US contractors (Taipei Times). Plan Colombia was a $10 billion US counternarcotics effort; spray missions required State Department and Colombian approval (AP).

cases.conditions: US aid for coca eradication by air. The mix used was 44% glyphosate, 1% Cosmoflux and 55% water, per the 2013 settlement (Al Jazeera); the Roundup label gives 29% as the upper limit.
cases.community: More than 4 million acres were sprayed over about two decades, with a peak of 172,000 hectares in 2006 (Taipei Times). A study by economist Daniel Mejia using 2003-2007 medical records found more skin problems and miscarriages in sprayed districts (Taipei Times, Al Jazeera). More than 2,000 Ecuadoran farmers and fishers sued, saying spray drifted across the border and damaged crops, animals and health. The farmers' group Forccofes counted about 15,000 border families, about 10,000 along the San Miguel river most affected.
cases.outcome: In September 2013 Colombia agreed to pay Ecuador $15 million and keep spraying at least 10 km from the border for a year; Ecuador dropped its International Court of Justice case. A US jury in April 2017 awarded nothing to the first six farmers; the remaining claims later ended in a confidential settlement with DynCorp. Plan Colombia fumigation ended in 2015 (International Rights Advocates), the year the WHO's cancer agency reclassified glyphosate (Taipei Times).

Aurelio Burgos Blacutt, over the shooting of an unarmed man on 29 January 2002, had not been carried out by June 2002 (Washington Post).

Not counted: 13 coca growers dead in the 1998 Joint Task Force conflict and the wider total of 10 in 2001-2002, because WOLA does not say who killed them; Andres Condori, where the unit is only 'implicated'; the 57 growers the Permanent Human Rights Assembly counts since 1987; and security personnel who died (3 in 1998, 4 in Sacaba in January 2002).

cases.title: Chapare Coca Eradication by US-Paid Forces
cases.point: Chimoré, where Expeditionary Task Force bases are and where shots were fired on 6 December 2001

lenders.name: US Embassy Narcotics Affairs Section, State Department (aid)
lenders.role: Pays, feeds and clothes the Expeditionary Task Force of about 1,500 former soldiers, $100 a month each, plus about $200,000 a month of other costs (Washington Post, June 2002). Funded the Joint Task Force and UMOPAR police (WOLA).

lenders.name: USAID (grant)
lenders.role: Funded alternative development that required total eradication. In a 1998 survey, 67% of participants saw no benefit and 19% suffered losses (WOLA).

cases.conditions: Under Bolivia's Dignity Plan, launched in 1998, coca was uprooted by force, with the aim of ending illegal Chapare coca by 2002. The eradication forces were paid for by the US (WOLA, Washington Post).
cases.community: WOLA reports ten coca growers killed and at least 350 injured or detained in 2001-2002. Ramón Pérez was killed by Joint Task Force fire on 27 September 2001. On 15 November 2001 at Senda 6, Expeditionary Task Force members fired on a crowd, killing three. Nilda Escobar Aguilar died from a tear-gas canister on 16 October 2001. Union leader Casimiro Huanca was fatally wounded on 6 December 2001 at the union compound in Chimoré. Fructuoso Herbas lost a leg after being shot. Over eight months the human rights ombudsman attributed at least four killings and more than 50 beatings, clubbings and thefts to the task force (Washington Post).
cases.outcome: Decree 26415 was suspended in February 2002 after mediation and jailed union leaders were released (Refworld). lvwhy.project: Donor money paid to slaughter the remaining pigs and to bring in replacements.

cases.title: Haiti's Creole Pig Slaughter
cases.point: Hinche, central Haiti, as a marker for the countryside (approximate; the slaughter was nationwide)

lenders.name: United States (USAID), with Mexico and Canada
lenders.role: The eradication agreement had a $23 million budget, of which the US spent $15 million; Canada and Mexico gave money and staff through IICA (Multinational Monitor, written by a Washington Office on Haiti staff member). The Christian Science Monitor also gives $23 million for a United States-Mexican-Canadian-Dominican programme to slaughter the remaining pigs.

lenders.name: USAID (grant)
lenders.role: Set the payment schedule for pigs and funded repopulation, run by the Interamerican Institute for Cooperation in Agriculture (Multinational Monitor; Christian Science Monitor).

cases.conditions: Money paid to slaughter the pigs left after African swine fever reached Haiti in late 1978. The project, PEPPADEP, began in 1981. Haiti's government carried out the slaughter.
cases.community: Haiti had about 1.2 million pigs. Most of the loss came before or apart from the funded slaughter: the Christian Science Monitor says fever is believed to have killed two-thirds; the US Library of Congress country study says fever hit about a third and peasants sold or slaughtered another third in panic; the Multinational Monitor says 500,000 to 600,000 died of fever. The funded programme killed what remained, over 400,000 pigs (Multinational Monitor), leaving officially none by 1982. Tied to the programme: $9.3 million was set aside for owners, about $70 to $90 a pig, some owners said they were pressed to sell pigs worth $200 or more for about $15, and those affected by later slaughters got nothing (Multinational Monitor). Pigs were about 30% of peasant income and served as savings. Development officials said a drop in rural school attendance of 25 to 50 percent 'corresponds to' the eradication (Christian Science Monitor). Only about 40,000 replacement pigs existed in 1986; critics said they needed feed and care peasants could not afford.
cases.outcome: Farmers said they were not fairly paid, or not paid at all (Library of Congress). The official pig count rose from zero in 1982 to about 500,000 by 1989 (Library of Congress).

cases.community: Antonio Alves, 35, spent 11 days in jail in Antonina for cutting a tree to repair his mother's home in Quara Quara; three of its five cabins stood empty, and he said people left because they could no longer hunt and gather. lenders.name: HSBC
lenders.role: UK bank. Global Witness estimates that loans and services to seven Sarawak groups in 1977-2012 earned about US$130 million. Shin Yang: US$33.63 million in loans, including US$3.6 million in 2004 to the owners' investment company. WTK: nearly US$40 million in credit since 1990. Sarawak Oil Palms: US$25.6 million in 2003, and principal banker 2002-2011. Ta Ann: US$17.65 million, latest November 2004. Samling: US$88 million in credit lines by 2001. Six new loans worth US$25 million since 2004. The clearing described dates from 2005 onward, after these loans.

cases.conditions: HSBC's 2004 forest policy required clients to be on course to 70% certified operations by 2009. Global Witness found none of the Sarawak clients it checked held an FSC certificate.
cases.community: Global Witness reports: Shin Yang's clearing in Ulu-Belaga in 2005-2010, on land proposed as a 135,000-hectare national park of which under 10% stayed unlogged by February 2012, with alleged destruction of ancestral grave sites; a villager said armed men shot livestock after complaints. Sarawak Oil Palms drained and cleared peat forest in 2005-2009, including about 1,400 hectares on the proposed Mud Volcano park; communities say the lease came without their consent or pay, and two sued in 2012. WTK's oil palm arm served an eviction notice in Ulu Niah. Sarawak lost 10% of its forest in 2005-2010; about 5% remains intact.
cases.outcome: HSBC said it would end relationships with non-compliant clients as soon as contracts allowed. HSBC appears to have dropped Samling in 2010.

lenders.name: Westpac Bank PNG
lenders.role: No loan document is public. Oxfam infers one: floating charges registered for Westpac since 1995 over WTK Realty and Vanimo Forest Products secure 'advances and accommodation', which Oxfam says most likely means a credit line or loan, over 19 years. These charges are on WTK companies, not the Turubu lease holder, and Oxfam calls WTK's lease links 'anything but direct'.

cases.conditions: The Turubu Special Agricultural and Business Lease went to Sepik Oil Palm Plantation Ltd on 2 September 2008, covering 116,840 hectares for 99 years.
cases.community: Over 50 landowning groups were affected. People were told the lease was for palm oil, but saw logging. Tracked 2012 log shipments were worth almost US$6.5 million; one village said each of three clans got 10,000 kina in 2009 and others said they got nothing. Residents reported food shortages, polluted water, health problems and destroyed sacred sites. A woman in Turubu Bay said fish had almost disappeared because of oil from machines (Oxfam). Oxfam Australia's chief executive wrote that logging pollution killed fish and prawns and damaged the reef.
cases.outcome: A Commission of Inquiry found only four of 42 such leases reviewed had real landowner consent and a viable project, and recommended revoking the Turubu lease (Oxfam, 2014). WTK made no public comment. Westpac said it could not comment on alleged links because of customer confidentiality, and that it was prepared to leave customers over risk (RNZ, SBS).

lenders.name: 44 banks, among them Sumitomo Mitsui, Mizuho, Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi UFJ, HSBC, Royal Bank of Scotland, Rabobank, Standard Chartered, BNP Paribas, Deutsche Bank, Citibank and JP Morgan Chase

cases.conditions: General corporate lending and underwriting, not tied to a plantation.
cases.community: RAN and partners interviewed 41 workers on two certified Lonsum plantations in North Sumatra in September-October 2015. Four boys aged 13, 16, 16 and 19 worked as harvesters' helpers and said they had left school; the 19-year-old said he began at 12. Three workers at one plantation reported using Gramoxone (paraquat). Of nine women interviewed, seven sprayed or fertilised; those fertilising reported no protective gear. Indofood itself reported 21,000 litres of paraquat used in 2015. Hundreds of farmers were evicted in 2013 for the Sei Merah plantation (Forests & Finance).
